title: Facebook
summary:
Checking a Page's activity meant switching into that Page, which kept admins from liking and commenting as themselves. I joined the work from Underbelly, on a project that was already underway.

The panel they already used became the place to look. All activity in one tab, a tab per Page beside it, and a dot instead of a count. Opening a tab changes the list. It does not change who is logged in. Settings, which I took on once that direction was set, decide which Pages can notify an admin and which categories.

This version did not reach a public launch. I was not in that decision.

media.caption: The volume of reaction on a Page, then the choice to turn the rest off. Comments, likes, tags, posts, and shares can each be silenced without swapping the whole account.
The home feed, then the notification panel. New comments, mentions, and follows arrive in one stream until an admin filters by Page.
Page notification settings. Which Pages can send notifications, and which categories for that Page.
An exploration of the panel, including a Highlights stack. That direction did not survive critique.
Suggested for You, in the feed and in notifications. Separate from the Page notification panel.

title: Square
summary:
A spike in seller-reported phishing traced back to Square's own email. Every department had built its own template, and no two messages looked alike, so a seller could not tell a real one from a fake.

Those templates were componentized into seven thematic buckets with the design system team. The highest-volume emails moved first, so other teams adopted the system on their own. Sender rules cover dynamic content, plain-text fallbacks, and messages that still read as Square when images are blocked.

media.caption: A seller email in the inbox, then the same kind of message before and after the system. Recognition happens before anyone follows the link into the dashboard.
Two templates from the seven buckets: a card added to a wallet, and a card on its way. Same sender, same structure, different job.
Header, body, and footer as separate pieces. Seven buckets, one library, so every seller email can be recognized as Square, including the plain-text fallback and the version with images blocked.

title: Slide
summary:
Claims at Slide were a phone call, about 20 minutes each. A week in Tampa with the executive team mapped how agents triaged a loss, and that script became a flow a policyholder could finish on the site.

Choosing the loss type and giving Slide the minimum it needs to start replaced the call. The average claim dropped to 8 minutes. In four months the flow processed more than 10,000 claims, and 45% of them never touched a phone.

The sprint secured a $300k contract extension and the green light to design the application. Months later Slide raised $35M to expand through Florida.

media.caption: The claim on a laptop and a phone. Welcome, contact, then the loss type: the questions an agent used to read aloud on a 20-minute call.
The loss-type step at the two sizes a policyholder actually uses. Weather, water, fire or smoke, theft, other property damage, and liability, each with the definition from the phone script.

The rest of the product around that step: filing a claim through to a claim number, tracking it, making a payment, and previewing the policy. The intake is the piece that took 45% of claims off the phone.

title: TRUE-See
summary:
Photographing a wound meant leaving the chart, signing into a second app, and rebuilding the patient. The EHR-agnostic path pulls the list from the record, then capture, wound type, measure, and save stay in one pass.

As sole designer, the work was the research, the workflow, and the interface, including the Bootstrap system the app shipped on. Photos can be found by hashtag, such as #ulcer, instead of selecting from a pile of unassigned images.

The photograph is color-calibrated and certified, so a clinician can compare the same wound later without guessing at the phone's color.

media.caption: The path into the camera, the capture screen, and the photograph it is for. The first session has to clear permissions, the camera, and the first upload.
Patient list to camera. The old path signed a clinician into the EHR, then into TRUE-See, and asked for the patient again. The new path starts from the list the record already has.
The photograph the workflow is built around: a calibrated, certified image a clinician can trust, then send back to the chart, share, or assign a wound type.

title: Arcoscan
summary:
Biometric age verification, productized as a step inside onboarding. A face outline and one instruction, open your mouth, prove a person is present, and the flow continues.

The scan had lived as a technology demo built with SRI. The product version keeps the person in the same session: camera access, the prompt, a result, then the next screen, instead of a handoff to a separate verification site.

media.caption: The check is the prompt. Open your mouth, hold still inside the outline, and continue. Age and liveness are the same step, so onboarding does not stop for a second vendor.

title: Peridot
summary:
Search across interviews. Peridot transcribes the call, pulls themes, pain points, and feature requests, and answers a question with the sentence and the minute it came from.

Calls can come from Zoom, Google Meet, Otter, or Dovetail, with surveys, support tickets, and sales calls beside them. A highlight or a quote can be opened without an account, and an insight can be turned into a Linear ticket.

The research is not used to train the models. Transcription and the write-up run through the providers, and the citation stays attached to the source.

media.caption: The product is the citation. An insight opens at the minute it was said, with the quote beside the recording, so a stakeholder gets the clip instead of a deck.

title: ELFI
summary:
Students were qualifying for an ELFI loan and leaving before the application. Pre-qualification to application start sat at about 40%. The rate view was the place to look: repayment plans, fixed and variable, and an APR, with the total behind a click.

I tested the application with students, then tried the fixes as versions inside the product. What shipped puts repayment plans and interest rates on separate screens, the total in the table, and a plain explanation of APR.

Pre-qualification to signup moved from 40% to 67%.

media.caption: How much to refinance, then the payment the calculator recommends, before the application is finished.

The old ELFI form asked for the whole refinance on one page, including income, a co-signer, and the loan amount. The new one is four steps, starting with the school, and a student can move between them.
Amount and term on one side. Monthly payment, APR, total interest, and the payment timeline on the other, including a deferred grace period, before the application is finished.
